etymology: Clipped from proper respect (or proper recognition), used as a plural like dues; African-American vernacular and hip-hop speech of the late 1980s, widespread by the early 1990s in give props, mad props, and props to my crew. Rappers used it on record and in album shout-outs to credit mentors, DJs, and neighborhoods. The underlying word is proper (Latin proprius, one’s own), which in older English meant "fitting, due."
biblical_def: Props is credit given where credit is due: "Props to the drummer." "I gotta give you props for that." Hip-hop made the word a small ceremony of honor — a rapper naming the DJ who taught him, the block that raised him, the elder who opened a door. The Christian observation is that this is one of the most biblical habits in the whole Gen X vocabulary. Scripture commands it in older words: "Render therefore to all their dues … honour to whom honour" (Rom 13:7). "Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king" (1Pe 2:17). Believers are to be "in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10), and "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3). The one turn Scripture adds is direction: props are for giving, not for fishing. "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). A culture that demands respect becomes a culture of pride; a household that gives it freely becomes a household of love. And all lesser props point upward, to the Lord who gave every gift that anyone ever earned credit for, and whose "Well done" is the only praise that lasts. A father can say to his son: give props quickly and generously — to your mother first, to your teachers, to the teammate who made you look good — and never ask for them. The Lord sees, and He keeps the books.
webster_summary: Hip-hop slang (late 1980s, from proper respect) for credit and honor given where due; Scripture commands the same habit — honour to whom honour (Rom 13:7) — and forbids fishing for it (Pro 27:2).
webster_full: PROPS, n. pl. (Gen X slang, late 1980s, hip-hop / African-American vernacular) Due respect, credit, recognition. "Props to my DJ." "You gotta give him props — he earned it."
Phrases: give props, mad props (1990s New York intensifier), much props; clipped from proper respect / proper recognition.
Kin to the hip-hop shout-out: naming one’s teachers, crew, and neighborhood on record; the opposite is dissing.
Webster 1828: PROPER, a. [Latin proprius, supposed to be allied to prope, near.] 1. Peculiar; naturally or essentially belonging to a person or thing; not common. …
Decode for parents: "props" is honor rendered; teach your children to give it freely and never to demand it.
scriptures: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
corruption_summary: Props is honor rendered, a habit Scripture commands; the corruption comes when respect is demanded rather than given, and props become a currency of pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Respect demanded. The word has a shadow. In the same streets that coined props, respect could become something a young man insisted on with his fists, and the lack of it a reason for violence. That is pride wearing honor’s clothes. Scripture never tells a man to collect honor; it tells him to pay it (Rom 13:7) and to prefer others in it (Rom 12:10). The man who must have his props has made himself the center of the room, and "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2) is God’s plain rebuke.

Honor rendered. The best of hip-hop’s props culture was a form of gratitude: naming the DJ, the mentor, the mother who held it together. That is the fifth commandment in a new accent, and Peter widens it: "Honour all men" (1Pe 2:17). A Christian family should be a place where props flow in every direction — parents to children, children to parents, brother to sister — and all of it upward to God, who gave every gift anyone was ever praised for.
roots_summary: Latin proprius (one’s own) → English proper (fitting, due) → proper respect → hip-hop props (late 1980s) → mad props; Scripture: honour to whom honour (Rom 13:7).
roots_lines: Latin proprius — one’s own, particular
English proper — fitting, belonging, due
Late 1980s African-American vernacular and hip-hop: props, clipped from proper respect
1990s: give props, mad props spread through rap records, radio, and campus speech
Biblical honor: render to all their dues (Rom 13:7); in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10)
usage: "Big props to Coach Johnson for sticking with us all season."
Honour to whom honour (Rom 13:7) — props, rendered God’s way.
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth (Pro 27:2).

etymology: Origin uncertain: usually explained as a clipping of definite or definitive ("the definitive thing"), though some trace it to Jamaican English death used as an intensifier. It was current in New York hip-hop speech by the early 1980s for "excellent, first-rate." Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons founded Def Jam Recordings in 1984 (LL Cool J, the Beastie Boys, Public Enemy), and HBO’s Def Comedy Jam (1992) kept the word in national circulation.
biblical_def: Def means the real thing, the best of its kind: a def beat, a def rhyme, a def pair of sneakers. If the usual explanation is right and it comes from definite, the word carries a happy idea inside it — that some things are not just good but settled, unmistakably excellent. The Christian observation is that Scripture has a great deal to say about excellence, and it is careful about where the word lands. "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Psa 8:1). David calls the godly "the excellent, in whom is all my delight" (Psa 16:3). Paul prays that believers would "approve things that are excellent" (Php 1:10), and after listing the gifts of the Spirit he shows the church "a more excellent way" — the way of love (1Co 12:31). He even gives the Christian mind its own list of what is truly def: "whatsoever things are true … honest … just … pure … lovely … of good report" (Php 4:8). The danger in the word is small but real: a child raised to call a sneaker definitive may never be taught what is definitively good. The cure is to train taste, not to ban slang — to teach children to recognize excellence in a well-made thing and then to see in it a small reflection of the God whose name alone is excellent in all the earth. A father can say: son, you know a def beat when you hear one; learn to know a def life when you see one — true, honest, pure, and lovely — and learn the One who lived it first.
webster_summary: Hip-hop slang (early 1980s New York; Def Jam, 1984) for excellent, first-rate, probably from definite; Scripture trains the taste to approve things that are excellent (Php 1:10).
webster_full: DEF, adj. (Gen X slang, early 1980s, New York hip-hop) Excellent, first-rate, the genuine article. "That beat is def." "A def rhyme."
Probably clipped from definite / definitive; origin uncertain. Fixed in the culture by Def Jam Recordings (1984) and Def Comedy Jam (HBO, 1992).
Companions: fresh, fly, phat; the Gen X opposites are wack and bunk.
Webster 1828: DEFINITE, a. 1. Having certain limits; bounded with precision; determinate; as a definite extent of land; definite dimensions; definite measure. …
Decode for parents: "def" means unmistakably excellent; train your children’s taste so they can tell what truly is (Php 4:8).
scriptures: O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens.
But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight.
That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ;
But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: Def crowns the sneaker and the beat as definitive; Scripture keeps excellent first for God’s name and teaches the mind to approve what is truly excellent.
corruption_paragraphs: Taste without a standard. Every generation has a word for "the best," and every generation’s best is set by someone — a label, a radio station, a crowd. Def was coined by artists and quickly taken up by marketers; by the 1990s what was def was largely what was sold as def. The Christian is told to "approve things that are excellent" (Php 1:10), and that requires a standard outside the crowd. Paul supplies one in Php 4:8, and every item on his list can be applied to a song, a film, or a friend.

The excellent name. The Psalmist’s refrain, "how excellent is thy name in all the earth" (Psa 8:1), is where the language of excellence starts. Craftsmanship, rhythm, and wit are good gifts, and a well-made record can show the order God built into sound. But the most excellent way is love (1Co 12:31), and the most excellent One is Christ. A child who learns that keeps his slang and gains a scale to measure it by.
roots_summary: Probably English definite (Latin definire, to bound, settle) → early-1980s New York hip-hop def → Def Jam (1984) → mainstream; Scripture: how excellent is thy name (Psa 8:1).
roots_lines: Latin definire — to bound, to settle; English definite, definitive
Early 1980s New York hip-hop: def — excellent, the real thing (origin uncertain)
1984: Def Jam Recordings founded by Rick Rubin and Russell Simmons
1992: HBO’s Def Comedy Jam carries the word nationwide
Biblical excellence: approve things that are excellent (Php 1:10); a more excellent way (1Co 12:31)
usage: "That new LL Cool J tape is def."
Approve things that are excellent (Php 1:10) — a standard for what is def.
How excellent is thy name in all the earth! (Psa 8:1).

etymology: Short for bunkum, from Buncombe County, North Carolina: in 1820, during the Missouri Compromise debate, Congressman Felix Walker rose to give a long, irrelevant speech and explained that he was speaking "for Buncombe" — for the voters back home. Bunkum came to mean empty, showy talk; bunk (nonsense) was in use by the early 1900s, made famous by Henry Ford’s "History is more or less bunk" (1916 interview), and debunk followed in the 1920s. In late-1980s and 1990s hip-hop and teen speech bunk became an adjective: weak, lousy, worthless ("that party was bunk"). It is unrelated to bunk, a sleeping berth.
biblical_def: When a Gen X kid called something bunk, he meant it was weak, phony, or worthless: a bunk movie, a bunk excuse, a bunk deal. The word has an honest pedigree in American politics: it began as bunkum, the windy speech a congressman made "for Buncombe" County in 1820 — words that sounded important and said nothing. The Christian observation is that God has an unusually sharp ear for bunk. "In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury" (Pro 14:23). Our Lord warned that "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment" (Mat 12:36). Paul tells Timothy to avoid "profane and vain babblings" (1Ti 6:20) and warns the Colossians against "philosophy and vain deceit" (Col 2:8) — ideas that look impressive and are hollow inside. Through Jeremiah the LORD sets the false prophets’ dreams beside His own Word and asks, "What is the chaff to the wheat?" (Jer 23:28). So a child who can smell bunk has a gift worth training. The world is full of it: in advertising, in campaigns, in the confident voices on a screen. The trouble is that we are quick to detect bunk in others and slow to detect it in ourselves — our own excuses, our own boasts, our own religious talk with no obedience behind it. A father can say: good ear, son; now turn it on your own mouth first, and measure everything against the one Word that is never bunk.
webster_summary: Gen X slang (late 1980s) for weak, worthless, phony, from bunkum (Buncombe County, 1820) — empty talk; Scripture weighs every idle word (Mat 12:36) and asks, What is the chaff to the wheat? (Jer 23:28).
webster_full: BUNK, adj. and n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s) As adj., weak, lousy, worthless; as n., nonsense, humbug. "That excuse is bunk." "This party is bunk — let’s go."
Short for bunkum: from Buncombe County, N.C., after Rep. Felix Walker’s 1820 speech "for Buncombe"; debunk (1920s), to expose as false.
Henry Ford’s "History is more or less bunk" (1916); unrelated to bunk, a sleeping berth, as in bunk bed.
Webster 1828: BUNK, n. A case or cabin of boards for a bed; a word used in some parts of America.
Decode for parents: a child who can detect bunk has a good gift; teach him to turn it on his own words first.
scriptures: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Bunk is a good ear for empty talk; the danger is a cynicism that hears bunk everywhere except in its own mouth, and treats God’s Word as one more claim to debunk.
corruption_paragraphs: The cynic’s ear. Gen X grew up on advertising, Watergate, and televangelist scandals, and it learned to call bunk on nearly everything. Some of that was wisdom: "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15). But cynicism is not discernment. The man who debunks everything ends up believing nothing, and a heart that believes nothing is not wise — it is merely closed. Paul’s warning against vain deceit (Col 2:8) assumes there is a truth "after Christ" to hold on to.

Bunk at home. Our Lord’s word about idle words (Mat 12:36) is aimed first at the speaker, not the listener. The windy congressman of 1820 talked for applause; so do we, in smaller rooms. The labor that profits is obedience; the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury (Pro 14:23). The cure for bunk is not a sharper tongue but a truer one, filled with the wheat of God’s Word instead of the chaff of our own (Jer 23:28).
roots_summary: Buncombe County, N.C. (Rep. Felix Walker, 1820) → bunkum (empty talk) → bunk (nonsense, early 1900s) → debunk (1920s) → Gen X adjective bunk (worthless); Scripture: the chaff and the wheat (Jer 23:28).
roots_lines: 1820: Rep. Felix Walker speaks "for Buncombe" County, North Carolina, in the Missouri debate
19th-c. American bunkum / buncombe — empty, showy political talk
Early 20th c. bunk — nonsense (Ford, 1916); 1920s debunk
Late 1980s–1990s teen and hip-hop adjective: bunk — weak, lousy
Biblical measure: every idle word (Mat 12:36); vain babblings (1Ti 6:20)
usage: "That movie was bunk — I want my five bucks back."
Every idle word shall be given account of (Mat 12:36) — bunk is weighed in heaven.
What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD (Jer 23:28).

etymology: From trip (Middle English trippen, to step lightly; to stumble). The 1960s counterculture used trip for an LSD experience and tripping for being under the drug’s influence. By the late 1980s, African-American and hip-hop speech had turned trippin’ into "overreacting, acting irrationally, losing perspective" — "You trippin’!" — with no drug in view, and the phrase ran through 1990s rap, film, and school hallways; don’t trip meant "don’t worry about it."
biblical_def: "You trippin’" is the Gen X way of telling a friend he has lost his head: he is overreacting, imagining things, making a scene over nothing. "Why you trippin’ over a parking ticket?" The word’s history deserves a father’s attention: it was borrowed from the drug culture of the 1960s, where a trip was a mind taken out of itself by a chemical. By the time Gen X used it, it simply meant a mind taken out of itself by emotion. Scripture prizes the opposite. "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). "Be sober, be vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Pro 14:29), and "he that ruleth his spirit" is better "than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). James turns it into a rule for the hallway: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). The old meaning of trip — to stumble — is the honest one: the young man who flies off the handle has tripped over his own temper. But Christ is "able to keep you from falling" (Jud 1:24). A father can use the word gently: son, when you feel yourself trippin’, stop and pray before you speak; the sound mind is a gift God gives, not a mood you have to manufacture.
webster_summary: Gen X / hip-hop slang (late 1980s) for overreacting or acting irrationally, from the 1960s drug trip; Scripture prizes the sound mind (2Ti 1:7) and the man slow to wrath (Pro 14:29).
webster_full: TRIPPIN’, v. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, African-American and hip-hop speech) Overreacting; acting irrationally; imagining things; losing one’s cool. "Calm down — you trippin’."
Also trippin’ over (fussing about), don’t trip (don’t worry about it); from 1960s trip, a drug experience.
Companions: buggin’, flippin’ out, freakin’ out.
Webster 1828: TRIP, v.i. To stumble; to strike the foot against something, so as to lose the step and come near to fall; or to stumble and fall. 1. To err; to fail; to mistake; to be deficient. …
Decode for parents: "you trippin’" means "you’ve lost your head"; teach the sound mind God gives (2Ti 1:7).
scriptures: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
corruption_summary: Trippin’ borrows the drug culture’s picture of a mind taken out of itself; Scripture calls for a sober, sound mind ruled by the Spirit, not by the passion of the moment.
corruption_paragraphs: A word from the drug culture. The trip of the 1960s was a deliberate unhinging of the mind, sought as a doorway to experience. By the 1990s the drug had dropped out of the word, but the picture remained: a mind that has slipped its moorings. That the slang was needed at all says something — a generation wanted a word for the person ruled by his own passions. Scripture names the remedy: be sober, be vigilant (1Pe 5:8), because the adversary hunts the unguarded mind.

Ruling the spirit. The Bible does not tell a young man never to feel anger or alarm; it tells him to rule them. He that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city (Pro 16:32). The Christian’s sound mind (2Ti 1:7) is not cold self-control but trust: a heart at rest in God has less reason to trip. When a friend says "you trippin’," a humble believer can take it as a brother’s rebuke and be slow to wrath (Jas 1:19).
roots_summary: Middle English trippen (step lightly, stumble) → 1960s drug trip → late-1980s hip-hop trippin’ (overreacting) → mainstream; Scripture: a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).
roots_lines: Middle English trippen — to step lightly; to stumble
1960s counterculture: trip, tripping — an LSD experience
Late 1980s African-American and hip-hop speech: trippin’ — overreacting, irrational
1990s: don’t trip, why you trippin’? in rap, film, and school hallways
Biblical remedy: slow to wrath (Pro 14:29); a sound mind (2Ti 1:7)
usage: "It’s just a B on a quiz — why you trippin’?"
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding (Pro 14:29).
God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but … of a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).

etymology: From bug. American slang bug, to annoy or pester, is recorded from the 1940s ("quit bugging me"); bug out, c. early 1950s military slang, meant to retreat in a panic, and bug-eyed described the wide stare of alarm. In New York hip-hop and street speech of the 1980s buggin’ (or buggin’ out) came to mean acting crazy, panicking, or losing one’s composure — "You buggin’!" — and it spread nationally through rap records and 1990s youth culture.
biblical_def: To be buggin’ is to be rattled, frantic, or acting crazy: "She’s buggin’ about the test." "You buggin’ — nobody took your Walkman." It is the word for a mind that has run ahead of the facts and started to panic. The Christian observation is that Scripture speaks to the buggin’ heart with remarkable tenderness. Jesus did not scold anxious disciples into calm; He gave them Himself: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you … Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid" (Joh 14:27). Paul turns worry into prayer: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Php 4:6). David says simply, "Fret not thyself" (Psa 37:1). Our Lord lifts tomorrow off our shoulders: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow" (Mat 6:34). And Isaiah gives the promise: "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isa 26:3). Notice what these texts do not say. They do not say the trouble is imaginary; they say God is bigger than it. The world’s answer to a buggin’ kid is "chill"; the gospel’s answer is a Person to trust. A father can say to an anxious daughter: you don’t have to stop feeling it before you pray; bring the whole mess to your Father, and let His peace keep your heart.
webster_summary: New York hip-hop slang (1980s) for panicking, acting crazy, or losing composure, from bug (to annoy) and bug out (to flee in panic); Scripture answers the frantic heart with prayer and perfect peace (Php 4:6; Isa 26:3).
webster_full: BUGGIN’, v. (Gen X slang, 1980s, New York hip-hop and street speech) Acting crazy; panicking; overreacting; losing one’s composure. "Relax, you buggin’."
Also buggin’ out; from American bug, to annoy (1940s), and military bug out, to retreat in a panic (c. early 1950s).
Older sense still alive: bugging, pestering ("Stop bugging your sister"). Companion: trippin’.
Webster 1828: BUG, n. In common language, the name of a vast multitude of insects, which infest houses and plants. …
Decode for parents: "buggin’" is anxiety out loud; meet it with prayer and the peace of Christ, not just "calm down."
scriptures: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
corruption_summary: Buggin’ names a mind that has outrun the facts; the world says chill, but Scripture brings the frantic heart to a Father who keeps it in perfect peace.
corruption_paragraphs: Anxiety without an address. The slang is honest: it admits that a young person can come unglued. What the culture lacks is anywhere to send the panic. "Chill," "relax," and "it’s not a big deal" ask the troubled heart to calm itself, which is exactly what it cannot do. Scripture gives anxiety an address: in every thing by prayer and supplication (Php 4:6). Even the command not to fret (Psa 37:1) comes with reasons outside ourselves — the LORD sees, the LORD judges, the LORD provides.

The peace that keeps. Our Lord distinguishes His peace from the world’s: "not as the world giveth, give I unto you" (Joh 14:27). The world gives distraction; Christ gives Himself. Isaiah’s promise (Isa 26:3) ties perfect peace to the mind stayed on God. A believer may still be buggin’ on a bad day, but he has somewhere to run, and a Father who does not demand that he calm down before he comes.
roots_summary: English bug (insect, pest) → American bug (to annoy, 1940s) and bug out (to flee in panic, c. 1950s) → 1980s New York buggin’; Scripture: be careful for nothing (Php 4:6).
roots_lines: English bug — an insect, a pest; something that gets under the skin
1940s American slang: bug — to annoy, to pester
c. early 1950s military slang: bug out — to retreat in a panic
1980s New York hip-hop: buggin’ — acting crazy, panicking
Biblical answer: let not your heart be troubled (Joh 14:27); perfect peace (Isa 26:3)
usage: "Mom, I’m buggin’ — I can’t find my retainer!"
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer (Php 4:6).
Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid (Joh 14:27).

etymology: From kill + -er, one who kills. The inverted sense, "excellent, formidable," goes back to 1930s swing-era jive (killer-diller, a sensational tune or performer) and to the show-business boast that a comic "killed" an audience. Gen X made it a stock adjective in 1980s surf, skate, and teen speech — killer waves, a killer party, killer as a one-word verdict — and the computer trade coined killer app by the late 1980s.
biblical_def: In Gen X speech killer was praise: a killer wave, a killer guitar solo, a killer deal. "How was the concert?" "Killer." The word works the way bad and wicked work in slang — by flipping a dark word into a compliment. The Christian observation is not that a teenager who says killer is bloodthirsty; it is that a culture which makes death its highest compliment has grown careless about death. God has not. "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13) guards the image of God in every man. Our Lord named the first killer plainly: the devil "was a murderer from the beginning" (Joh 8:44), and he still comes "to steal, and to kill, and to destroy" (Joh 10:10). The gospel then tells the darkest use of the word in history: men "killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead" (Act 3:15). The world’s worst killing became the world’s life, because Christ came "that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly" (Joh 10:10). Words shape what we laugh at and what we admire: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Pro 18:21). A father need not police every killer his son says about a skateboard trick; but he can teach him that the word was borrowed from the enemy’s trade, and that the most excellent thing in the world is not a killer but a Life-giver.
webster_summary: Gen X surf, skate, and teen slang (1980s; from 1930s jive killer-diller) for excellent, formidable; a death-word turned compliment, set against the Life-giver who came that we might have life (Joh 10:10).
webster_full: KILLER, adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s, surf, skate, and teen speech) Excellent, formidable, outstanding. "Killer waves at the point today." "That solo was killer."
Antecedents: 1930s swing-era killer-diller; show-business "he killed" (was a hit). Compounds: killer app (late 1980s), killer deal.
Kin to the inversion slang of bad, wicked, and later sick: a dark word flipped into praise.
Webster 1828: KILLER, n. One who deprives of life; he or that which kills.
Decode for parents: "killer" just means great; but teach why death-words became compliments, and Who actually gives life.
scriptures: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
corruption_summary: Killer turns the devil’s trade into a compliment; Scripture names the murderer from the beginning and crowns instead the Prince of life, whom men killed and God raised.
corruption_paragraphs: The inversion habit. Bad, wicked, killer, and later sick share a pattern: the darker the word, the higher the praise. Part of this is simple youthful exaggeration; part of it is a culture that finds evil more interesting than good and death more thrilling than life. Isaiah pronounced woe on those "that call evil good, and good evil" (Isa 5:20). Slang inversion is not the same sin, but it trains the ear in the same direction, and a family does well to notice it.

The Prince of life. The deepest answer to killer is Peter’s sermon in Solomon’s porch: they "killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead" (Act 3:15). The devil is the true killer (Joh 8:44); Christ is the true life (Joh 10:10). A Christian can still call a wave killer, but he knows that death is an enemy, not a compliment, and that the last enemy has been defeated by an empty tomb.
roots_summary: Middle English killen (to strike, slay) → killer (one who kills) → 1930s jive killer-diller → 1980s surf and teen killer (excellent); Scripture: the Prince of life (Act 3:15).
roots_lines: Middle English killen — to strike, to slay; killer — one who kills
Show-business "to kill" an audience — to be a smash hit
1930s swing jive: killer-diller — a sensational tune or performer
1980s surf, skate, and teen speech: killer — excellent; late-1980s killer app
Biblical counterword: the murderer from the beginning (Joh 8:44) vs. the Prince of life (Act 3:15)
usage: "Dude, that was a killer ollie."
The thief cometh … to kill; Christ came that we might have life (Joh 10:10).
Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21).

etymology: Origin uncertain: often traced to hyperbole (Greek, "a throwing beyond"), and also to 1920s American underworld slang, where hype meant a swindle and hyped up (from hypo, a hypodermic needle) meant stimulated. By the 1960s hype meant extravagant promotion. Hip-hop made it double-edged in the late 1980s: Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back) warned against media spin, while the same scene used hype as an adjective for exciting, energetic ("the crowd was hype").
biblical_def: Hype has two faces in Gen X speech. As a noun it means inflated promotion — the hype around a movie, a sneaker, a prizefight. As an adjective it means exciting, charged up: "That show was hype." Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) captured the first sense for a generation: the headlines, the ads, and the image-makers will mislead you. The Christian observation is that this is sound biblical counsel. "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21). "Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God" (1Jn 4:1). Proverbs describes the man who hypes himself: "Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain" (Pro 25:14) — big thunderheads over a dry field. John names the engine underneath all of it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1Jn 2:16), which advertising has always known how to stir. And Jeremiah names the only thing worth boasting about: "let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:24). There is one Name that never disappoints its billing; the gospel is the only announcement in history that turned out bigger than the advance notice. A father can say to his son: don’t believe the hype — not the world’s, and not your own; but believe the Word, and boast in the Lord.
webster_summary: Gen X / hip-hop slang for inflated promotion (n.) or exciting, charged up (adj.), possibly from hyperbole; Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) echoes Scripture’s prove all things (1Th 5:21).
webster_full: HYPE, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s–1990s; hip-hop) As n., exaggerated promotion, buzz; as adj., exciting, energetic, charged up. "Don’t believe the hype." "The crowd was hype."
Hyped / hyped up, excited; to hype, to promote extravagantly. Possibly from hyperbole; compare 1920s hype (swindle) and hypo (hypodermic).
Public Enemy, "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988): the slogan of media skepticism for a generation.

Webster 1828: HYPERBOLE, n. hyper’boly. [Gr. excess, to throw beyond, to exceed.] In rhetoric, a figure of speech which expresses much more or less than the truth, or which represents things much greater or less, better or worse than they really are. …
Decode for parents: teach your children to test the hype — the world’s and their own — and to boast only in the Lord.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Hype is the art of making things look bigger than they are; Scripture tests every claim, exposes the boaster as clouds without rain, and reserves glorying for knowing the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Clouds without rain. Hype is the economy of the promise that does not deliver: the movie that was not as good as the trailer, the product that was not as life-changing as the ad, the celebrity whose image outran his character. Proverbs saw it three thousand years ago (Pro 25:14). Public Enemy’s warning was right as far as it went; the Christian adds that the human heart is also a hype machine, and we oversell ourselves most of all.

Glory rightly placed. Jeremiah forbids the three great self-promotions — wisdom, might, riches (Jer 9:23) — and permits one boast: that a man knows the LORD (Jer 9:24). Here is the only thing that cannot be overhyped. The gospel did not overpromise; the empty tomb outran every expectation. Teach children to discount the world’s hype, distrust their own, and spend their excitement on what will bear its weight.
roots_summary: Greek hyperbole (a throwing beyond) and 1920s hype / hypo → 1960s promotional hype → Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) and the adjective hype; Scripture: prove all things (1Th 5:21).
roots_lines: Greek hyperbole — a throwing beyond; exaggeration (one proposed source)
1920s American slang: hype — a swindle; hyped up — stimulated (from hypo, hypodermic)
1960s: hype — extravagant publicity
1988: Public Enemy, "Don’t Believe the Hype"; hip-hop adjective hype — exciting
Biblical test: try the spirits (1Jn 4:1); glory only in knowing the LORD (Jer 9:24)
usage: "Everybody said the sequel was amazing — don’t believe the hype."
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1Th 5:21).
Let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me (Jer 9:24).

etymology: From amp, the mid-20th-century clipping of amplifier, itself from amplify (Latin amplificare, to enlarge). Amped (also amped up) for "excited, energized, fired up" was current in 1980s California surf and skate speech — "I’m so amped for this swell" — and spread through 1990s extreme-sports and teen culture. A secondary sense, "wired on stimulants," also circulated, and a parent should know it.
biblical_def: To be amped is to be fired up, buzzing with anticipation: amped for the concert, amped for the big game, amped to paddle out. The picture is an electric guitar plugged into an amplifier with the knob turned all the way up. The Christian observation is that God is not against energy; He made it, and He commands it in the right direction. "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11). "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10); "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23). The question is what does the amplifying. Paul sets two sources of a lifted mood side by side: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). The world amps itself on noise, caffeine, crowds, and sometimes worse; the Christian is filled from another source, and it does not crash the next morning. "They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary" (Isa 40:31). Notice that Isaiah’s amplifier is waiting — the opposite of the rush. A father can rejoice with a son who is amped for a good thing, and then teach him where lasting fire comes from: not the volume knob, but the Spirit of God, who turns a quiet heart into a burning one and keeps it burning.
webster_summary: Gen X surf and skate slang (1980s, from amp, amplifier) for excited, fired up; Scripture wants the fervor (Rom 12:11), but from the Spirit rather than from excess (Eph 5:18).
webster_full: AMPED, adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s, California surf and skate speech) Excited, energized, eager. "I’m so amped for this weekend."
Also amped up; from amp, short for amplifier, as in turning a guitar amp all the way up.
Companions: pumped, stoked, psyched; a secondary sense, "wired on stimulants," parents should recognize.
Webster 1828: AMPLIFY, v.t. [Latin amplifico; of amplus and facio, to make large.] 1. To enlarge; to augment; to increase or extend, in a general sense; applied to material or immaterial things. …
Decode for parents: rejoice in a child’s fire, and teach him the difference between being amped by excess and filled with the Spirit.
scriptures: Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Amped celebrates energy turned all the way up; Scripture commends fervor but asks what does the amplifying — excess and noise, or the Spirit of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Borrowed voltage. A generation raised on stadium rock and energy drinks learned to treat excitement as something switched on from outside — a louder speaker, a faster board, a stronger stimulant. The trouble with borrowed voltage is the crash. Paul sets wine and the Spirit side by side (Eph 5:18) because both lift a man out of his ordinary self; only one lifts him toward God and leaves him better the next day.

Fervent in spirit. The Christian life is not meant to be tepid. Paul wants believers fervent (Rom 12:11); the Preacher wants work done with might (Ecc 9:10); the apostle wants every chore done heartily as to the Lord (Col 3:23). The fuel is unexpected: waiting upon the LORD (Isa 40:31). The young man who has learned to be still before God is the one who runs and does not grow weary.
roots_summary: Latin amplificare (to enlarge) → English amplify → amplifier / amp → 1980s surf and skate amped (fired up); Scripture: fervent in spirit, filled with the Spirit (Rom 12:11; Eph 5:18).
roots_lines: Latin amplus (large) → amplificare — to enlarge
English amplify; 20th-c. amplifier, clipped to amp
Rock-band picture: the amp turned all the way up
1980s California surf and skate speech: amped — excited, fired up
Biblical fervor: fervent in spirit (Rom 12:11); renewed strength (Isa 40:31)
usage: "We’re all amped for the youth retreat!"
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord (Rom 12:11).
Be not drunk with wine … but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).

etymology: From pump (Middle Dutch pompe), to raise water by suction. Bodybuilders spoke of "the pump," the swollen feeling of a muscle after lifting, made famous by the documentary Pumping Iron (1977) with Arnold Schwarzenegger. Pumped / pumped up for "excited, energized" was common by the early 1980s, and Saturday Night Live sealed it with Dana Carvey and Kevin Nealon’s Austrian bodybuilders Hans and Franz (from 1987), who had come to "pump you up."
biblical_def: Pumped means excited, ready, fired up: pumped for the game, pumped about a new job. The word came out of the weight room — the swelling of a worked muscle — and Hans and Franz on SNL (1987) turned it into a national joke about vanity and biceps. The Christian observation is that the joke was well aimed. Bodily strength is a gift, and Paul is not against exercise, but he ranks it: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come" (1Ti 4:8). Notice the order. The muscles fade; godliness lasts into eternity. Paul did train his body, but for the race, not the mirror: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection" (1Co 9:27). Real strength in Scripture comes from outside a man. "He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength" (Isa 40:29). "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Php 4:13) — a verse about contentment in want, not a slogan for the bench press. And Nehemiah tells weeping Israel where to find a lasting pump: "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). A father can lift weights with his son and enjoy every rep; then he can tell him: be pumped about good things, train hard, and remember that the strongest man in the room is the one who knows he is weak and leans on Christ.
webster_summary: Gen X slang (early 1980s; the weight-room pump, SNL’s Hans and Franz, 1987) for excited, fired up; Scripture ranks bodily exercise below godliness and finds strength in the joy of the LORD (1Ti 4:8; Neh 8:10).
webster_full: PUMPED, adj. (Gen X slang, early 1980s onward) Excited, energized, eager; also, swollen and muscular from a workout. "I’m pumped for the championship."
Also pumped up; from bodybuilders’ "the pump" (Pumping Iron, 1977).
SNL’s Hans and Franz (Dana Carvey and Kevin Nealon, from 1987) parodied it: they had come to "pump you up." Companions: amped, psyched.

Webster 1828: PUMP, n. [The Latin bombus is of the same family, as is the Eng.bombast.] 1. A hydraulic engine for raising water, by exhausting the incumbent air of a tube or pipe, in consequence of which the water rises in the tube by means of the pressure of the air on the surrounding water. …
Decode for parents: enjoy the excitement and the training, and teach that godliness, not muscle, is profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).
scriptures: For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
corruption_summary: Pumped comes from the mirror of the weight room; Scripture honors training but ranks godliness above muscle and locates real strength in the joy of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The mirror. Hans and Franz were funny because they were true: a generation discovered the gym and, with it, a new vanity. The body became a project and the mirror a judge. Scripture does not despise the body — it is the temple of the Holy Ghost — but it refuses to let the body become the god. Bodily exercise profiteth little (1Ti 4:8), and the man who spends more hours on his biceps than on his Bible has his profits upside down.

Strength from outside. Paul trained like an athlete for a purpose beyond himself (1Co 9:27). Isaiah’s promise (Isa 40:29) is to the faint, not the fit. Philippians 4:13, so often printed on gym shirts, was written by a prisoner about being content in hunger and plenty. The believer’s strength is the joy of the LORD (Neh 8:10) — a strength that does not shrink when the workouts stop and the years come.
roots_summary: Middle Dutch pompe → English pump → bodybuilders’ "the pump" (Pumping Iron, 1977) → Gen X pumped (excited) → Hans and Franz (1987); Scripture: the joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10).
roots_lines: Middle Dutch pompe → English pump — to raise or force by suction
Bodybuilding: "the pump" — the swell of a worked muscle; Pumping Iron (1977)
Early 1980s: pumped / pumped up — excited, energized
1987 onward: SNL’s Hans and Franz parody the gym culture
Biblical strength: godliness profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8); the joy of the LORD (Neh 8:10)
usage: "We play the Eagles Friday night — I’m pumped!"
Bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).
The joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10).

etymology: Origin uncertain; a short shout of greeting and attention long current in American street speech. In 20th-century America it was strongly associated with Philadelphia — the Rocky films (from 1976) made "Yo, Adrian!" a national catchphrase — and with New York hip-hop, where it served as greeting, attention-getter, and all-purpose sentence opener or tag. MTV’s Yo! MTV Raps (1988–1995) carried it into suburban living rooms across the country.
biblical_def: Yo is the shortest sentence in Gen X: a greeting ("Yo, what’s up?"), a call across the street ("Yo, Mike!"), an attention-grab before a point ("Yo, listen to this"). It is a word that calls a name and expects an answer. The Christian observation is that Scripture is full of exactly that exchange, and in it God is always the One calling first. "The LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). In the night at Shiloh, "the LORD called Samuel: and he answered, Here am I" (1Sa 3:4). When Isaiah heard the Lord asking, "Whom shall I send?" he answered, "Here am I; send me" (Isa 6:8). And to His redeemed people God says, "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine" (Isa 43:1). That is the gospel’s yo: the Creator calling a sinner by name, not to scold but to claim. The word itself is harmless — a Christian can say "yo" to his friends a hundred times a day. Paul’s only rule for greetings is that they carry grace: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6). A father can teach his children that the way they call to people matters, and that the most important call they will ever hear is God’s, in His Word and through His preachers. When He calls, the right answer is Samuel’s: "Here am I."
webster_summary: Gen X greeting and attention-call (Philadelphia and New York street speech; Rocky, 1976; Yo! MTV Raps, 1988); harmless in itself, it echoes the Bible’s pattern of God calling by name and man answering, Here am I (1Sa 3:4).
webster_full: YO, interj. (Gen X slang, 1970s–1990s, Philadelphia and New York street and hip-hop speech) Hey; hello; listen. "Yo, Mike!" "Yo, check this out."
Also a sentence tag ("That was crazy, yo"); carried nationwide by the Rocky films and Yo! MTV Raps (1988–95).
Exact origin uncertain; the call predates hip-hop in American street speech. Companion greeting: wassup.
No entry in Webster 1828; as a greeting the word is 20th-century American street speech.
Decode for parents: "yo" is a harmless hello; use it to teach that God calls His children by name (Isa 43:1).
scriptures: And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
That the LORD called Samuel: and he answered, Here am I.
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: Yo is a harmless call; its only danger is a habit of casualness that never learns to answer when the Lord calls — Scripture’s pattern is God calling by name and man replying, Here am I.
corruption_paragraphs: Calling without answering. A word like yo carries no sin in itself; the only caution is the culture of constant casualness it can belong to, where every call is a shout across the street and no call is ever weighty. Children raised that way may hear God’s summons in the preaching of the Word as one more "yo" to ignore. Samuel had to be taught by old Eli to recognize the voice (1Sa 3:4); our children need the same patient teaching.

The God who calls first. The Bible’s story is a story of calls: to Adam hiding (Gen 3:9), to Samuel sleeping, to Isaiah undone in the temple (Isa 6:8). In each case God speaks first, and grace comes with the call. "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine" (Isa 43:1) is the warmest greeting in the world. A believer can say yo to a friend all day; he says "Here am I" to only One.
roots_summary: Origin uncertain → American street call (Philadelphia, New York) → Rocky (1976) → hip-hop and Yo! MTV Raps (1988) → universal greeting; Scripture: I have called thee by thy name (Isa 43:1).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; a short shout of greeting and attention
Mid-20th c.: Philadelphia and New York street speech
1976 onward: the Rocky films make "Yo, Adrian!" a catchphrase
1980s hip-hop; Yo! MTV Raps (1988–1995) takes it into the suburbs
Biblical call and answer: Where art thou? (Gen 3:9); Here am I (1Sa 3:4)
usage: "Yo, you coming to youth group tonight?"
The LORD called Samuel: and he answered, Here am I (1Sa 3:4).
I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine (Isa 43:1).

etymology: A running-together of what’s up?, a long-standing American greeting immortalized by Bugs Bunny’s "What’s up, Doc?" (1940) and clipped to wassup and sup in 1980s–90s urban and hip-hop speech. The drawn-out, tongue-wagging Wassuuup! became a global catchphrase through Budweiser’s "Whassup?" television ads, first aired in December 1999 and adapted by director Charles Stone III from his short film True (1998), in which a circle of friends greet one another by phone.
biblical_def: Wassup is "what’s up?" squeezed into one word — and, after Budweiser’s ads of 1999, stretched into a shout: Wassuuup! It is a greeting that sounds like a question but rarely waits for an answer. The Christian observation is that God asks what’s up and means it. To the hiding Adam He said, "Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9) — not because He lacked the information, but because Adam needed to say it. To Elijah, collapsed in a cave after a great victory and a great fear, "the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?" (1Ki 19:9) — the tenderest what’s up in Scripture, given after bread, sleep, and before a still small voice. The church is called to ask the same way. "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4). "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). None of that is possible if wassup is only a noise. The ad was funny because the friends shouted into their phones and never said anything at all. A father can teach his children a small, holy habit: when you say wassup, stop long enough to hear the answer — you may be the way God asks a hurting friend, What doest thou here?
webster_summary: Contraction of "what’s up?", made a global catchphrase by Budweiser’s "Whassup?" ads (Dec 1999); a greeting that rarely waits for an answer, set beside the God who asks, What doest thou here? (1Ki 19:9).
webster_full: WASSUP, interj. (Gen X slang; American greeting, peaking 1999–2001) Hello; how are you; what is happening? "Wassup, man?" Drawn out as Wassuuup!
Spellings: whassup, wazzup, sup. From what’s up?; compare Bugs Bunny’s "What’s up, Doc?" (1940).
Budweiser "Whassup?" ads, from December 1999, adapted by Charles Stone III from his short film True (1998).
No entry in Webster 1828; the contraction is late-20th-century American speech.
Decode for parents: "wassup" is a fine greeting; teach your children to wait for the answer and to care what it is.
scriptures: And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Wassup asks a question it does not wait to hear answered; Scripture shows a God who asks and listens, and calls His people to bear one another’s burdens.
corruption_paragraphs: The question without a listener. The Budweiser friends shouted Wassup into the phone, tongues out, and hung up having said nothing — which was the joke. Much modern friendship has the same shape: a constant stream of greetings, likes, and check-ins with no one waiting for an answer. Paul’s rule (Php 2:4) asks more: look on the things of others. A greeting is meant to be the doorway to that care, not a substitute for it.

God’s what’s up. When Elijah ran from Jezebel and lay down in despair, the Lord did not shout at him; He fed him, let him sleep, and then asked, "What doest thou here, Elijah?" (1Ki 19:9). Then He listened to the whole complaint and answered it. That is how the church asks wassup: with bread in hand, ready to weep with them that weep (Rom 12:15) and to bear the burden (Gal 6:2).
roots_summary: "What is up?" → American greeting what’s up? ("What’s up, Doc?", 1940) → wassup → Budweiser’s "Whassup?" (1999); Scripture: What doest thou here, Elijah? (1Ki 19:9).
roots_lines: English what is up? — what is happening?
American greeting what’s up?; Bugs Bunny’s "What’s up, Doc?" (1940)
1980s–1990s urban and hip-hop speech: wassup, sup
December 1999: Budweiser’s "Whassup?" ads (Charles Stone III) make it a global catchphrase
Biblical greeting with a listener: Where art thou? (Gen 3:9); bear one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2)
usage: "Wassuuup!" — every high school hallway, spring 2000.
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others (Php 2:4).
What doest thou here, Elijah? (1Ki 19:9) — a what’s up that waited for the answer.

etymology: Short for "twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week." Recorded in American sports and street slang by the mid-1980s for "all the time, constantly," it spread with all-night convenience stores, ATMs, and round-the-clock services, and was nationwide by the early 1990s, later stretched to 24/7/365. The never-closed world it names arrived with cable news (CNN, 1980) and, by the late 1990s, the always-on internet.
biblical_def: 24/7 means all the time, without a break: "She texts him 24/7." "This job is 24/7." It began as a store sign and became a way of life — the always-open shop, the always-on news, and at last the always-on phone. The Christian observation is that only One is truly 24/7. "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep" (Psa 121:4). God’s mercies are not rationed by business hours: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lam 3:22-23). And He invites His people into a holy kind of constancy — "Pray without ceasing" (1Th 5:17), and the blessed man meditates in God’s law "day and night" (Psa 1:2). But here is the turn: God does not ask His creatures to be 24/7 in the way He is. He built rest into the week before there was a store to keep open. "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God" (Exo 20:9-10). "The sabbath was made for man" (Mar 2:27). A culture that never closes is a culture trying to be God, and it exhausts its children. "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late … for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). A father can say to a son who is grinding 24/7, or scrolling 24/7: you are not the one who keeps the world running; the Lord does. Pray always, work hard six days, and rest on the seventh, trusting the One who never sleeps.
webster_summary: Gen X slang (1980s, from "twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week") for constantly, nonstop; only God neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psa 121:4), and He built a sabbath into His creatures’ week (Exo 20:10).
webster_full: 24/7, adv. and adj. (Gen X slang, mid-1980s–present) All the time; constantly; around the clock. "He plays that game 24/7." "A 24/7 job."
Read "twenty-four seven"; from "twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week." Extended: 24/7/365.
Spread with all-night stores, ATMs, cable news (CNN, 1980), and the late-1990s always-on internet.
No entry in Webster 1828; the numeral shorthand is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: the world never closes; teach your children that only God is 24/7, and that He commanded us to rest.
scriptures: Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
corruption_summary: 24/7 is the creed of a world that never closes; Scripture reserves sleepless watchfulness for God alone and gives His creatures the gift of a weekly rest.
corruption_paragraphs: Playing God with the clock. A civilization that keeps its stores, screens, and offices open around the clock is quietly claiming an attribute that belongs to God: He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep (Psa 121:4). Men who try to match Him end up anxious and exhausted. The Psalmist calls it vain to rise early and sit up late eating the bread of sorrows (Psa 127:2); the always-on worker and the always-on teenager are proving him right every night.

Constant prayer, weekly rest. Scripture has its own 24/7: pray without ceasing (1Th 5:17), meditate day and night (Psa 1:2), mercies new every morning (Lam 3:23). But it pairs that constancy with a command to stop. The sabbath (Exo 20:10) is a weekly confession that God runs the world and we do not. A family that rests one day in seven, phones down and Bibles open, is preaching that sermon to its children.
roots_summary: "Twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week" → mid-1980s sports and street slang 24/7 → 1990s nationwide → the always-on phone; Scripture: He neither slumbers nor sleeps, and giveth His beloved sleep (Psa 121:4; Psa 127:2).
